{{Short description|Principle in computer science}}
In [[computer science]] and [[quantum physics]], the '''Church–Turing–Deutsch-Wolfram principle''' ('''CTDW principle''') is a stronger, physical form of the [[Church&ndash;Turing thesis]] articulated in separate works by [[Stephen Wolfram]]<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Copeland
 |first1=B. Jack
 |last2=Shagrir
 |first2=Oron
 |title=The Church-Turing Thesis
 |journal=Communications of the ACM
 |volume=62
 |issue=1
 |pages=66–74
 |date=December 2018
 |doi=10.1145/3198448
 |url=https://doi.org/10.1145/3198448
 |access-date=1 March 2026
}}</ref> and [[David Deutsch]]<ref>{{cite web|last=Nielsen|first=Michael|title=Interesting problems: The Church–Turing–Deutsch Principle|date=16 April 2004 |url=http://michaelnielsen.org/blog/interesting-problems-the-church-turing-deutsch-principle|accessdate=10 May 2014}}</ref> in 1985.

The principle states that a [[Turing completeness|universal]] [[computer|computing device]] can [[simulation|simulate]] every [[physical process]].

==History==

A formulation of the principle was given by [[Stephen Wolfram]] in February 1985. In ''Undecidability and Intractability in Theoretical Physics''<ref>{{cite journal
 |last=Wolfram
 |first=Stephen
 |date=25 February 1985
 |title=Undecidability and Intractability in Theoretical Physics
 |journal=Physical Review Letters
 |volume=54
 |issue=7
 |pages=735–738
 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.54.735
}}</ref>, Wolfram wrote that

{{Quote|text="[U]niversal computers are as powerful in their computational capacities as any physically realizable system can be, so that they can simulate any physical system."}}

Wolfram states that such a principle would hold provided that physical systems have a finite density of information and that information can be transmitted only at a finite rate in a finite-dimensional space.

Later in 1985, [[David Deutsch]] stated the principle with respect to [[finitary]] machines and processes.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Deutsch|first=D.|year=1985|date=8 July 1985|title=Quantum theory, the Church–Turing principle and the universal quantum computer|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society|volume=400|issue=1818|pages=97–117|doi=10.1098/rspa.1985.0070}}</ref> He observed that [[classical physics]], which makes use of the concept of [[real number]]s, cannot be simulated by a [[Turing machine]], which can only represent [[computable real]]s. Deutsch proposed that [[quantum computer]]s may obey the principle, assuming that the laws of [[quantum mechanics]] can completely describe every physical process.

An earlier version of this thesis for classical computers was stated by Alan Turing's friend and student [[Robin Gandy]] in 1980.<ref>Gandy, R. (1980). Church’s thesis and principles for mechanisms. ''Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics'' (101), 123–148</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Kaznatcheev |first=Artem |title=Falsifiability and Gandy's variant of the Church-Turing thesis |journal=Theory, Evolution, and Games Group Blog |year=2014 |url=https://egtheory.wordpress.com/2014/09/01/falsifiability-and-gandys-variant-of-the-church-turing-thesis/ |accessdate=23 July 2018}}</ref>

A similar thesis was later stated by [[Michael Freedman]] in an early review of [[topological quantum computing]] with [[Alexei Kitaev]], [[Michael J. Larsen]], and [[Zhenghan Wang]], known as the Freedman–Church–Turing thesis:<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Freedman |first1=Michael H. |title=Topological Quantum Computation |date=2002-09-20 |last2=Kitaev |first2=Alexei |last3=Larsen |first3=Michael J. |last4=Wang |first4=Zhenghan|eprint=quant-ph/0101025 }}</ref>

{{Quote|text="All 'reasonable' computational models which add the resources of quantum mechanics (or quantum field theory) to classical computation yield (efficiently) inter-simulable classes: there is one quantum theory of computation."}}

This thesis differs from the Church–Turing–Deutsch-Wolfram thesis insofar as it is a statement about computational complexity, and not computability.
